content_html:
Living with an Evolved Brain

Possible Solutions to Mismatch Problems

Evolutionary psychology and evolutionary psychiatry both emphasise that many of our difficulties arise from an evolved brain running in a rapidly changed environment. There is no single “fix” for this, but there are multiple levels at which we can intervene: personal habits, relationships and culture, and the wider technological and policy environment. The goal is not to fight our evolved machinery, but to understand it well enough to design surroundings and practices that support rather than exploit it.

Personal level: working with, not against, the machinery

Psychoeducation in evolutionary terms.

Understanding anxiety, low mood, jealousy, or compulsive urges as overactive or misdirected defence and reward systems—not as personal failings—can itself reduce shame and improve engagement with treatment. Evolutionary psychiatry explicitly advocates using evolutionary explanations to distinguish between protective responses and true defects, and to clarify why vulnerabilities exist.

Evidence-based therapies as cognitive re-engineering.

Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), and mindfulness-based approaches can be seen as systematic ways to retrain prediction, threat appraisal, and habit learning. Large meta-analyses show that CBT is effective across anxiety and depressive disorders, in part by modifying distorted interpretations and breaking maladaptive reinforcement loops. From an evolutionary perspective, these methods help tune systems that evolved for a different world to the realities of the present one.

Managing supernormal stimuli.

The concept of supernormal stimuli describes artificially exaggerated cues (for example, ultra-processed foods, pornography, or gambling apps) that drive stronger responses than anything in ancestral environments. At a personal level, one “solution” is to put friction between yourself and such stimuli: limiting exposure, using website blockers or time limits, and deliberately choosing simpler, less engineered rewards (whole foods, offline hobbies, face-to-face contact).

Designing a supportive micro-environment.

Because self-control is finite, intentionally structuring one’s immediate environment—removing high-sugar snacks from the home, keeping phones out of the bedroom, turning off non-essential notifications—can be more effective than relying on moment-to-moment willpower. This is consistent with behaviour change models that stress the importance of “choice architecture” and environmental cues in shaping behaviour.

Relational and cultural level: steering norms and scripts

Shaping sexual and body norms.

Research on objectification and sexualisation shows that cultural standards strongly influence how bodies are perceived and how individuals experience their own attractiveness and worth. Recognising that some media and advertising operate as supernormal sexual stimuli suggests concrete responses: media literacy education, more diverse and realistic body representation, and subcultures that emphasise mutuality, consent, and relational qualities over narrow appearance cues.

Dress, status, and social signalling.

Recent work in person perception argues that dress is a fundamental channel through which observers infer traits and status. Because evolved status and coalition-detection mechanisms are so sensitive, unrealistic or rigid appearance norms can produce chronic social comparison and anxiety. Cultural “solutions” include relaxing dress codes, broadening acceptable styles, and decoupling competence or moral worth from specific clothing or beauty standards.

Rebuilding slow, face-to-face social structures.

Studies of contemporary hunter–gatherer groups highlight dense, supportive, face-to-face networks as a key feature of ancestral human life. In contrast, loneliness and social isolation are now major risk factors for mental and physical illness. Creating modern analogues of small, stable groups—through community organisations, clubs, and repeated offline gatherings—is one way to reduce mismatch at the social level.

Narratives that acknowledge biology without fatalism.

Evolutionary explanations can be misused to justify harmful behaviour (“wired that way,” “boys will be boys”). Leading authors in evolutionary psychology and psychiatry explicitly warn against this, emphasising that understanding ultimate causes does not dictate what is morally acceptable. A healthier narrative treats evolved drives as constraints and tendencies that culture, law, and personal ethics can and should shape.

Structural and technological level: redesigning the wider environment

Public health and food environments.

The evolutionary mismatch explanation for obesity and metabolic disease has already informed policies that target the food environment: taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages, restrictions on marketing ultra-processed foods to children, and reformulation targets to reduce salt, sugar, and trans fats. These are examples of system-level attempts to realign an engineered environment with bodies adapted to scarcity.

Attention-extractive technologies.

Many digital platforms use variable-ratio reinforcement schedules, personalised recommendations, and infinite scroll—all known to strongly engage dopaminergic reward pathways. Policy proposals now include limiting dark patterns, mandating more transparent choice architectures, and age-appropriate design codes that restrict some engagement-maximising features for children and adolescents. At scale, such regulations can reduce how aggressively technology exploits evolved vulnerabilities.

Work, stress, and economic precarity.

Chronic job insecurity, long working hours, and low autonomy are major predictors of anxiety and depression. From an evolutionary standpoint, they represent persistent, uncontrollable threats to status and survival signals. Structural “solutions” therefore include labour policies that improve job control and security, living-wage standards, and social safety nets—interventions that directly alter key mismatch drivers rather than treating only downstream symptoms.

Integrating evolutionary psychiatry into services.

Evolutionary psychiatry proposes that services routinely assess potential mismatches (sleep schedules, social rhythms, chronic stressors) and not just symptoms, and that they distinguish more carefully between defence and defect when deciding how aggressively to suppress a symptom. This does not replace medication or psychotherapy, but it can redirect some clinical effort toward environmental and lifestyle interventions that target root mismatches.

What a “solution” really looks like

There is no switch that turns off mismatch. Instead, the emerging consensus in evolutionary medicine is that progress comes from working at all these levels at once:

  • Individually, by learning how our minds work and deliberately structuring our habits and immediate environments.
  • Interpersonally and culturally, by reshaping the scripts and norms that channel our evolved drives.
  • Structurally, by redesigning systems—food, tech, work, housing—that currently monetise or exacerbate mismatch.

In that sense, the “solution” is not to transcend biology, but to become better custodians of it: using knowledge about our evolved vulnerabilities to build worlds in which those vulnerabilities are less relentlessly exploited and more often supported.
